- If sentiment is strongly positive (e.g., >0.7) and forecast is rising steadily, reduce forecast slope to avoid over-optimism.  
- If sentiment turns negative (e.g., <0.1) and forecast is high, apply downward bias or reduce trend magnitude.  
- After a sharp price spike, model often overshoots — cap forecast peak at 1.5x prior high or adjust downward by 5–10% of spike magnitude.  
- When sentiment is flat (near 0.0) and history shows low volatility, model tends to over-smooth — introduce slight upward jitter or adjust mean to match recent low volatility trend.  
- If true outcome shows mean reversion (e.g., after 3+ consecutive high peaks), reduce forecast slope and add slight downward drift.  
- For 30-day horizon, if forecast is consistently >10% above true outcome, apply a 10–15% downward correction unless sentiment strongly supports continuation.  
- If sentiment history shows recent negative spikes (e.g., -0.1 to -0.3), model often ignores it — reduce forecast by 2–5% for next 3–5 days.  
- When true outcome deviates from forecast by >15% in first 5 days, adjust forecast to align with early sentiment shifts — don’t wait for full 30-day trend.
